title: The Depression, the post office and Eugene Wright's band
summary: He carried mail while playing with Eugene Wright's young band, and was forced out over holding two jobs.

bands.name: Eugene Wright and his Dukes of Swing

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: Somebody on the phone. No, but what I wanted to know is like, you were like a professional musician for a long time and then, when was it you had, you said you, the music got bad and you went into this other business.
Well, well I was doing the depression. Things didn't straighten out.

Yeah, things didn't straighten out. First I started carrying mail out of the old post office. But I got a little break. There came a call for a trombone player and they didn't know I was an old man and I didn't know these young kids. There was Eugene Wright, Eugene Wright and his Dukes of Swing. So they had, I'd say 90% of the gigs around there. And they had so much work. And I was carrying mail out of the old post office. I'd just lay my uniform on the bed when I reached, when I came home, you know. And it seemed like I didn't lay down about two minutes before the long clock. I had to be down there for a quarter after five. And sometimes they'd play at three o'clock. So I made a lot of money. I used to just put my whole check, my whole check and the post office in the bank. Just walk right across the street, the Continental. But it liked to kill me, see. I had to spend that money. You worked too hard. Yeah, I worked too hard. See, what I should have done, I could have lived off of just playing music. And the regular spots during the war was paying $150.75. So I could have gotten one of those and made myself satisfied. But I was trying to make all the money. And I paid for it, see. So I stayed with them fellas. I went to the call for a horse. I went out there. They were all 18, 17, 19, 20 years old. They were always in school together. So they kept me. I was in a fella named John, in John Avance's place, which is this horn I have now. He, I distolled two horns from me. And we were playing the same band at that time. And so he said, well, take mine because I'm going down tomorrow and buy me new. And he said, I don't like this one. So he said, I loaned it to you. So he loaned me his horn and I still have it. That's 25 years ago. He loaned it to me and then he gave it to me. Yeah. So I haven't bought a new horn in over 25 years.
Then you gave up the post office after all.

Yeah, I gave up the post office. Well, I had a little trouble. I'd take my leave absence for a month. I was having trouble in my stomach. But I still was trying to play whenever they'd get a job, I'd play. So the fella by the name of Henderson right there, he was a stool pigeon. He saw me going to play one night. And my supervisor's name was Gross. So he told Gross about it. And so I received a telegram stating that it is a Liz that you have two jobs. And they asked me to resign. Well, I'm fat. I got about six, seven thousand dollars a bank, you understand? Yeah. And so I'm fat. So I just take my thing, got my bag out the locker and what we would call the big house, the main post office. And so I had to write out a statement. And I just stated that it is a Liz that I have two jobs, which I don't. I could, if I cared, to get a letter from my physician, family doctor. And I just went on to say that it wasn't so. So the fella said, well, it may have repercussions. I said, well, if it had repercussions, I'm telling the truth. I don't have two jobs, see? And the bad thing about it, some of them clerks were waiting tables at the Palmer House. See what I'm talking about? But nobody snitched on them, they snitched on me.
But when they had two jobs or not, I don't see how they would make any difference.
Yeah, well, they don't want you to have no two jobs. I wasn't even working with a post office.
That's ridiculous. It's your own business if you want to work five days.
